alt: A two-by-two grid. Primary quantitative: your own closed-question questionnaire results. Primary qualitative: transcripts of your own unstructured interviews. Secondary quantitative: census or crime figures. Secondary qualitative: diaries, letters, news articles and social media posts.
caption: Who produced the data and what form it takes are two separate questions.

alt: Recorded crime shrinks from all crimes, to those reported by victims, to those recorded by police; the rest is the hidden dark figure. Atkinson argued that suicide statistics depend on how coroners interpret clues such as notes and the manner of death.
caption: Official figures depend on decisions by victims, police and officials.

alt: Four types of secondary evidence, each with examples, strengths and limitations: official statistics, historical and personal documents, digital sources and media content, with named studies by Laslett, Thomas and Znaniecki, and the Glasgow University Media Group.
caption: Every type of secondary evidence has a strength to use and a limitation to criticise.

alt: Four numbered steps: read the labels, find and quote the exact figure with its unit, describe the pattern, then question the evidence. The routine works for summaries of studies, diagrams, tables, charts and graphs.
caption: Labels, figure, pattern, problems: the same routine for every source.

alt: Stacked bars of how often three age groups read news online: 16–29 is 71% daily, 20% weekly, 9% rarely; 30–49 is 58%, 27%, 15%; 50 and over is 33%, 30%, 37%. Below, an identified figure, a described trend and four problems with the evidence.
caption: Pick one figure, describe the trend, then question how the data was collected.

alt: Three worked chains, each naming a problem, linking it to the source and stating its effect: volunteers over-represent strong views; an online survey misses older non-users so the age gap looks smaller; a changed definition of unemployment breaks up a trend.
caption: Name it, link it, state its effect.
